title: Principles of Community-Centred Care with Emphasis on Comprehensive Health Care
path: Principles of Community-Centred Care with Emphasis on Comprehensive Health Care

headings.title: Introduction to Community-Centred Care
headings.content: Community-centred care shifts the focus of health service delivery away from isolated hospital beds and into the everyday environments where people live, work, and age. This approach recognizes that health is shaped by social, economic, and environmental factors far beyond the clinic walls. For nursing students in Nigeria, understanding this model means looking past acute disease management to see the wider community as the primary client. Care delivered in this context prioritizes disease prevention, health promotion, and rehabilitation at the grassroots level. By working directly within local settlements, nurses can identify patterns of illness that trace back to common environmental sources, such as contaminated water supplies or inadequate waste disposal.

headings.title: Core Principles of Primary Health Care
headings.content:
Primary Health Care serves as the bedrock of an effective health system, anchored by principles established at the Alma-Ata declaration. These tenets ensure that health services are not a privilege for the wealthy, but a universal right.

- **Equitable distribution**: Essential health services must reach all segments of the population regardless of wealth or location.
- **Community participation**: Local populations must be actively involved in planning, implementing, and evaluating their own health programs.
- **Intersectoral collaboration**: Health sectors must work alongside agriculture, education, and housing to address root causes of poor health.
- **Appropriate technology**: Medical methods and equipment must be scientifically sound, culturally acceptable, and economically affordable for the community.

headings.title: Comprehensive Health Care: Components and Scope
headings.content: Comprehensive health care goes beyond treating immediate physical symptoms by integrating promotion, prevention, curative, and rehabilitative services into a seamless continuum. In a Nigerian primary health care centre, this spans maternal and child health, routine immunizations, provision of essential drugs, and mental health support. Nurses must address the whole person within their family and community structure, rather than focusing on a single isolated disease entity. When managing a patient with chronic hypertension, comprehensive care requires assessing dietary habits, home stress levels, and access to medication, alongside checking blood pressure readings.

headings.title: Community Assessment and Health Needs Identification
headings.content: Before planning any intervention, community health nurses must conduct a systematic assessment to identify actual health deficits and hidden risks. This process involves gathering epidemiological data, holding focus groups with village leaders, and observing environmental sanitation conditions firsthand. A common pitfall is assuming outside professionals know community priorities better than the residents themselves. Direct observation and listening to local narratives reveal whether high malaria rates stem from a lack of mosquito nets or stagnant drainage ditches near homes. Accurate data collection ensures that limited health resources target the most pressing local vulnerabilities.

headings.title: Cultural Competence and Local Engagement
headings.content: Cultural competence requires nurses to acknowledge, respect, and integrate the beliefs, values, and traditions of the populations they serve. In multicultural settings like Nigeria, a failure to respect local customs can lead to community distrust and poor health service utilization. Nurses must collaborate with traditional birth attendants, village elders, and local faith leaders rather than dismissing indigenous practices outright. When health education respects local worldviews, community members become active partners in adopting healthy behaviors such as exclusive breastfeeding or hospital-based antenatal care.

headings.title: Intersectoral Collaboration and Sustainability
headings.content: Health cannot be achieved by the health sector working in isolation. Sustainable improvements require coordinated action across multiple fields, including education, agriculture, public works, and local government administration. For instance, reducing childhood malnutrition requires agricultural workers to boost crop yields, educators to teach nutrition in schools, and nurses to monitor growth charts. Furthermore, community programs must be designed to outlast short-term donor funding cycles. Sustainability relies on empowering local committees to take ownership of health projects, ensuring long-term maintenance and community self-reliance.
